nodes.title: Risk estimation and risk factor treatment in persons with type 2 diabetes mellitus
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the interplay between cardiovascular disease (CVD) and various health conditions, particularly focusing on ischemic heart failure (HF), cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It highlights that individuals diagnosed with ischemic HF are at high cardiovascular risk, necessitating secondary prevention strategies. In cancer patients, shared risk factors and biological mechanisms between cancer and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) are noted, emphasizing the importance of managing CVD risk to improve overall outcomes. The document also addresses the cardiotoxic effects of cancer treatments, the need for monitoring cardiac function during therapy, and the potential benefits of exercise in mitigating these risks.

Furthermore, it outlines the relationship between COPD and CVD, noting that COPD patients have a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality. The document details the shared risk factors between COPD and CVD, the impact of acute exacerbations on cardiovascular health, and the importance of screening COPD patients for ASCVD. It also discusses the challenges in diagnosing CVD in COPD patients and the implications of COPD medications on cardiovascular health. Overall, the document underscores the critical need for integrated management of cardiovascular and respiratory conditions to improve patient outcomes.

3.4.4.1 Diagnosis and screening
Signs or symptoms of cardiac dysfunction should be monitored
before and periodically during and after cancer treatment for earlydetection of abnormalities in patients receiving potentially cardio-
toxic chemotherapy. Detection of subclinical abnormalities using
imaging and measurement of circulating biomarkers (such as cardiactroponins and natriuretic peptides) is currently recommended.

strain, may precede a significant decline in LVEF.230/C0233
3.4.4.2 Prevention of cardiotoxicity and cardiovascular risk factors
RCTs of preventive therapy with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone sys-tem (RAAS) inhibitors and/or beta-blockers after trastuzumab or
anthracyclines have reported contradictory results.
230,234,235The
main benefits are less marked LV remodelling or a reduced decline inLVEF observed with cardiac magnetic resonance, but translation into
better outcomes remains speculative.
Exercise should be strongly advised. In particular, aerobic exercise is
considered a promising non-pharma cological strategy to prevent and/
or treat chemotherapy toxicity.

higher risk of CVD in survivors of ch ildhood cancer than in non-cancer
adult controls, and particularly in survivors of adult-onset cancer with
underlying ASCVD risk factors.237Therefore, aggressive management
of ASCVD risk factors in this population is recommended.
3.4.5. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a complex, pro-
gressive respiratory disorder and currently the fourth leading cause
of death worldwide. It is characterized by chronic airflow limitationwith respiratory symptoms and is associated with an increased
inflammatory response and abnormalities of the airways caused by
significant exposure to noxious particles or gases (mainly smoking).Although COPD is recognized and thoroughly investigated as a CVD
comorbidity, its role as an ASCVD risk factor is not well established.
Nevertheless, COPD patients have a two- to three- fold increasedrisk of CVD compared with age-matched controls when adjusted for
tobacco smoking. Patients with mild-to-moderate COPD are 8 /C010
times more likely to die from ASCVD than respiratory failure, havinghigher rates of hospitalization and death due to CVD, stroke, and
HF.

patients with electrocardiographic (ECG) evidence of myocardialinfarction are diagnosed with CVD.
240CVD mortality increases by
28%, and the frequency of non-fatal coronary events by 20%, for
every 10% decrease in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second(FEV1).
241Acute COPD exacerbations, mainly due to infections, are
frequent and are responsible for a four-fold increase of CVD
events.242The risk of both myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke
is increased during the 3 months after an acute exacerbation.243
The high prevalence of CVD in COPD patients may be explained
by the fact that both diseases share common risk factors, such assmoking, ageing, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia.
244Metabolicsyndrome and reduced PA is present in 34% of COPD patients, with
its most prevalent components being hypertension (56%), abdominal
obesity (39%), and hyperglycaemia (44%).245CVD may be caused by
hypoxia during exercise due to lung hyperinflation, high resting heart
rates, impaired vasodilatory capacity, and peripheral, cardiac, and
neurohumoral sympathetic stress. Atherosclerosis and coronaryartery calcification may be the result of oxidative stress, and reduc-
tions in antiaging molecules causing both lung and vascular ageing.
246
Systemic inflammation is prominent in COPD, with circulating bio-
markers in high concentrations and associated with increased mortal-
ity.247Troponin is elevated during an acute exacerbation of COPD,
and 10% of hospitalized patients meet the definition of acute myocar-dial infarction (AMI).
248B-natriuretic peptide level, if elevated,
increases the mortality risk.249
Systemic inflammation and oxidative stress caused by COPD pro-
mote vascular remodelling, stiffness, and atherosclerosis, and induce
a ‘procoagulant’ state that affects all vasculature types.250Cognitive
impairment and dementia due to cerebral microvascular damage iscorrelated with COPD severity; patients have a 20% increased risk
for both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, which may be up to
seven-fold higher following an acute exacerbation.
251PAD is present
in about 9% of COPD patients,252who have an almost doubled risk
of developing PAD,253as well as an increased prevalence of carotid
plaques related to the disease severity.254Finally, COPD is positively
associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm, regardless of smoking
status.255
Cardiac arrhythmias are common and may be due to the haemo-
dynamic effects (pulmonary hypertension, diastolic dysfunction, atrial
structural, and electrical remodelling) caused by the disease in combi-
nation with autonomic imbalance and abnormal ventricular repolari-zation.
256AF is frequent, directly associated with FEV1, usually
triggered by acute exacerbations of COPD, and an independent pre-
dictor of in-hospital COPD mortality.257,258COPD is also a risk fac-
tor for ventricular tachycardia independent of LVEF,259and for
sudden cardiac death independent of CVD risk profile.260
Unrecognized ventricular dysfunction is common in COPD,261
although HF is 3.8 times more common in COPD patients than incontrols.
262Patients with frequent acute exacerbations have a high
frequency of diastolic dysfunction; HFpEF risk is higher because of ahigh prevalence of hypertension and DM.
263
Considering these facts, it seems of upmost importance to screen
COPD patients for ASCVD and ASCVD risk factors, bearing in mindthat COPD affects the accuracy of CVD diagnostic tests. Achieving
adequate exercise is difficult, vasodilators for myocardial perfusion
scanning may be contraindicated because of the risk of broncho-spasm, and stress or transthoracic echocardiography is often dis-
turbed by poor ultrasound windows. Computed tomography
coronary angiography or magnetic resonance imaging may be alterna-tives, but remain expensive, time consuming, and not always
available.
The use of COPD medications (i.e. long-acting muscarinic antago-
nists and long-acting beta agonists) is not associated with overall CV
adverse events in patients with stable COPD. Olodaterol may reduce
the risk of overall CV adverse events and formoterol may decreasethe risk of cardiac ischaemia. Long-acting beta agonists may reduce
the incidence of hypertension, but may also increase the risk of HF,
so should be used with caution in HF patients.

In the section on COPD, it outlines the increased risk of CVD in COPD patients, noting that they have a higher likelihood of cardiovascular events and mortality compared to age-matched controls. It discusses the implications of acute exacerbations of COPD on cardiovascular health and the need for careful screening for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in COPD patients, considering the challenges posed by the disease on diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, it mentions the cardiovascular safety of COPD medications and their potential effects on heart health.

nodes.title: Communication of cardiovascular disease risk
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various health conditions and their associations with cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Key points include:

1. **Cardiotoxicity in Cancer Treatment**: It highlights the importance of monitoring cardiac function in patients undergoing potentially cardiotoxic chemotherapy, recommending imaging and biomarker assessments for early detection of cardiac dysfunction. Preventive strategies, including exercise and management of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors, are emphasized.

2. **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)**: The document outlines COPD as a significant risk factor for CVD, noting the increased mortality and hospitalization rates due to cardiovascular events in COPD patients. It discusses the shared risk factors between COPD and CVD, the impact of acute exacerbations, and the need for screening and management of cardiovascular risks in COPD patients.

3. **Inflammatory Conditions**: Chronic inflammatory diseases, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, are associated with increased CVD risk. The document suggests a low threshold for CVD risk assessment in these patients and advocates for similar preventive interventions as in the general high-risk population.

4. **Infections**: The document addresses the cardiovascular risks associated with infections like HIV and influenza, noting increased risks of cardiovascular events following respiratory infections. It also mentions the potential link between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis.

5. **Migraine**: It discusses the association between migraine, particularly migraine with aura, and increased risks of ischemic stroke and cardiac ischemic disease, highlighting the need for caution in contraceptive use among women with migraines.

6. **Sleep Disorders**: The document emphasizes the relationship between sleep disturbances, especially obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and increased CVD risk. It notes that while treatment for OSA has not significantly improved cardiovascular outcomes, lifestyle interventions are necessary.

7. **Mental Disorders**: It highlights the prevalence of mental health disorders in the general population and their association with increased CVD risk and reduced life expectancy. The document stresses the importance of screening for mental health issues in patients with CVD.

Overall, the document underscores the multifaceted relationship between various health conditions and cardiovascular risk, advocating for comprehensive screening and management strategies.

nodes.title: Potential risk modifiers
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various health conditions that increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). It highlights the significant impact of inflammatory conditions, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, which raises CVD risk by approximately 50%. Other inflammatory diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, and ankylosing spondylitis, are also mentioned, though with less robust evidence. The document emphasizes the importance of assessing CVD risk in patients with chronic inflammatory conditions and suggests that traditional risk reduction methods remain effective.

Infections, particularly HIV and influenza, are noted for their association with increased CVD risk, with specific statistics provided for HIV-related risks based on CD4 cell counts. The document also discusses the link between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis, although further research is needed to confirm the clinical benefits of treating periodontitis.

Migraine is identified as a prevalent condition that doubles the risk of ischemic stroke and increases cardiac ischemic disease risk, especially in those with aura. The document advises caution regarding combined hormonal contraceptives in women with migraines due to heightened vascular risk.

Sleep disorders, particularly obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), are associated with increased CVD risk, although treatment with positive airway pressure has not shown significant improvements in cardiovascular outcomes. The document stresses the need for comprehensive interventions, including lifestyle changes.

Lastly, mental disorders are highlighted as prevalent in the general population and significantly associated with CVD development and reduced life expectancy. The document calls for regular screening for mental health issues in CVD patients, as the onset of CVD can exacerbate mental health conditions and increase suicide risk.

nodes.title: Ethnicity
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various health conditions and their associations with cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Key points include:

1. **Inflammatory Conditions**: Chronic inflammation, particularly from rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, significantly increases CVD risk. Assessment of total CVD risk should be prioritized in these patients, considering disease activity.

2. **Infections**: HIV, influenza, and periodontal disease are linked to increased CVD risk. HIV raises the risk of lower extremity arterial disease (LEAD) and coronary artery disease (CAD), while influenza can exacerbate cardiovascular complications.

3. **Migraine**: Migraine is associated with a higher risk of ischemic stroke and cardiac ischemic disease, particularly in those with aura. The risk is compounded by factors like smoking and hormonal contraceptives.

4. **Sleep Disorders**: Sleep disturbances, especially obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), are correlated with increased CVD risk. Treatment for OSA has not shown significant improvement in cardiovascular outcomes, indicating the need for comprehensive lifestyle interventions.

5. **Mental Disorders**: Mental health issues are prevalent and linked to higher CVD risk. The document emphasizes the importance of screening for mental disorders in CVD patients and the need for integrated care.

6. **Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)**: NAFLD is associated with increased myocardial infarction and stroke risk, although its impact beyond traditional risk factors is less clear.

7. **Sex-Specific Conditions**: Conditions like pre-eclampsia and polycystic ovary syndrome in women are associated with elevated CVD risk. Early menopause also increases CVD risk.

8. **Erectile Dysfunction (ED)**: ED is linked to increased all-cause and CVD mortality, sharing common risk factors with CVD. Assessment of ED is recommended as part of CVD risk evaluation in men.

The document concludes with a call for individualized risk assessment and treatment strategies for these conditions to mitigate CVD risk.

Additionally, it emphasizes that patients with mental disorders often receive inadequate recognition and treatment for traditional CVD risk factors. 

The document further explores non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its association with increased CVD risk, while also mentioning the need for lifestyle recommendations for affected individuals. Lastly, it discusses erectile dysfunction (ED) in men, its multifactorial causes, and its significant association with increased CVD risk, advocating for CVD risk assessment in men presenting with ED. The document concludes with a mention of the importance of clear communication regarding treatment risks and benefits.

nodes.title: Frailty
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the relationship between mental disorders and cardiovascular disease (CVD), highlighting the uncertain mechanisms by which mental health issues contribute to increased CVD risk. It notes factors such as unhealthy lifestyles, socioeconomic stressors, and the effects of certain medications. The document also addresses barriers to healthcare access for individuals with mental disorders, including stigma and insufficient mental health literacy among providers. Additionally, it emphasizes that patients with mental disorders often receive inadequate recognition and treatment for traditional CVD risk factors.

The document further explores non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its association with increased CVD risk, while also mentioning the need for lifestyle recommendations for affected individuals. It covers sex-specific conditions, including obstetric issues like pre-eclampsia and pregnancy-related hypertension, which elevate future CVD risk. Non-obstetric conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome and premature menopause are also discussed in relation to CVD risk.

Erectile dysfunction (ED) is highlighted as a significant condition affecting men, with a strong correlation to CVD risk and common risk factors. The document suggests that men with ED should undergo CVD risk assessment and emphasizes the importance of lifestyle changes to improve both sexual function and cardiovascular health. Finally, it touches on the need for clear communication regarding treatment risks and benefits in managing these conditions.

................................................................... and benefits of individual treatment are the topic of this section. In all
scenarios where recommendations for individual interventions to
reduce risk are ‘strong’ (class I or IIa), it is important to realize thatmany patients who have received appropriate risk information often
(in up to 50% of cases, some studies suggest) consciously opt to
forego the proposed intervention. This applies not only to lifestylemeasures, but also to drug interventions. Apparently, what professio-
nals feel is sufficient risk reduction for a reasonable effort or initiation
of a drug with few side-effects does not always correspond topatients’ views. The reverse is also true: not only may some patients
at (very) high risk forego interventions, some patients with low-to-
moderate risk may be highly motivated to decrease their risk evenfurther. Hence, treatment recommendations are never ‘imperative’
for (very) high risk patients, nor are interventions ever ‘prohibited’
for patients at low-to-moderate risk. There is evidence that a higherproportion of women, compared to men, have a low awareness of
their CVD risk and the need for therapeutic interventions. This war-
rants efforts to improve awareness, risk assessment, and treatment inwomen.
52,346/C0351
4.2. Optimizing cardiovascular risk
management
4.2.1. Goals of clinicianpatient communication
Clinicians should provide a personalized presentation of guidelines toimprove understanding, encourage lifestyle changes, and support
adherence to drug therapy. Applying this in daily practice faces differ-
ent barriers.
352Patients’ ability to adopt a healthy lifestyle depends
on cognitive and emotional factors, the impact of a diagnosis or symp-
toms, socioeconomic factors, educational level, and mental health.
Perceived susceptibility to illness and the anticipated severity of theconsequences are also prominent components of patients’
motivation.
353
4.2.2. How to improve motivation?
Communication strategies such as mo tivational interviewing are use-
ful.354Consultation sessions may include a family member or friend,
especially for elderly patients. Connection is paramount: focus before
greeting; listen intently; agree on what matters most; connect with theperson’s story; and explore emotions.
355The OARS (Open-ended
questions, Affirmation, Reflective li stening, and Summarizing) principle
helps patients to present their perceptions, and clinicians to summa-rize. The SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Timely)
principle may help with setting goals for behavioural change.
353,356
Healthcare professionals must consi der capability, opportunity (physi-
cal, social, or environmental) and motivation for behavioural
change.357Multidisciplinary behavioural approaches that combine the
knowledge and skills of different caregivers are recommended.358
4.2.3. Optimizing drug adherenceMedication adherence ranges from 50% for primary ASCVD preven-
tion to 66% for secondary prevention.
359Physicians should consider
non-adherence in every patient and inquire non-judgmentally aboutit.
360Approximately 9% of cases of ASCVD in Europe can be attrib-
uted to poor medication adherence.361Contributors to non-
adherence include polypharmacy, complexity of drug/dose regimes,poor doctor-patient relationship, lack of disease acceptance, beliefsabout consequences and side-effects, intellectual/cognitive abilities,
mental disorders, physical limitations, financial aspects, and living
alone.
360,362/C0364Importantly, only substantial risk reduction moti-
vates patients for preventive drug treatment, which obviates the
need for appropriate risk communication.365,366Depression is
another important factor, and adequate treatment thereof improvesadherence.
367,368
Mobile phone applications may improve adherence to both medi-
cation and behavioural changes.369Their use is easy and probably
cost-effective.370
4.2.4. Treatment goalsIn the subsequent sections, different domains of individual treatment
are discussed. Table 6summarizes the treatment goals and some key
interventions for different categories of patients. For additional infor-mation on risk categories and the principle of a stepwise approach to
treatment targets, please refer to section 3.2.3.1 . For details on treat-
ment goals, how to achieve them, strengths of recommendations andlevels of supporting evidence, please go to the relevant subsections.
4.3.Optimizing lifestyle
4.3.1. Physical activity and exercise
PA reduces the risk of many adverse health outcomes and risk factors
in all ages and both sexes. There is an inverse relationship between
moderate-to-vigorous PA and all-cause mortality, CV morbidity andRecommendations for physical activity
Recommendations ClassaLevelb
It is recommended for adults of all ages to strive
for at least 150 - 300 min a week of moderate-
intensity or 75 - 150 min a week of vigorous-intensity aerobic PA, or an equivalent combina-
tion thereof, to reduce all-cause mortality, CV
mortality, and morbidity.
371,372IA
It is recommended that adults who cannot per-
form 150 min of moderate-intensity PA a week
should stay as active as their abilities and healthcondition allow.
373,374IB
It is recommended to reduce sedentary time to
engage in at least light activity throughout the
day to reduce all-cause and CV mortality andmorbidity.
375/C0377IB
Performing resistance exercise, in addition to
aerobic activity, is recommended on 2 or moredays per week to reduce all-cause
mortality.
378,379IB
Lifestyle interventions, such as group or individ-
ual education, behaviour-change techniques, tel-ephone counselling, and use of consumer-based
wearable activity trackers, should be considered
to increase PA participation.

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the importance of individual treatment and the challenges associated with patient adherence to recommended interventions for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction. It highlights that many patients, even those at high risk, may choose to forgo proposed treatments, which can include lifestyle changes and medications. The document emphasizes the need for improved awareness, particularly among women, regarding CVD risks and therapeutic options. It outlines strategies for optimizing clinician-patient communication to enhance understanding and motivation for lifestyle changes and medication adherence. Techniques such as motivational interviewing and the use of the OARS and SMART principles are recommended to facilitate effective communication and goal-setting. The document also addresses the factors contributing to medication non-adherence and suggests that mobile applications may help improve adherence. Additionally, it provides recommendations for physical activity to reduce health risks, emphasizing the importance of regular exercise and reducing sedentary behavior. Overall, the document aims to enhance cardiovascular risk management through personalized treatment approaches and effective communication strategies.

................................................................... and benefits of individual treatment are the topic of this section. In all
scenarios where recommendations for individual interventions to
reduce risk are ‘strong’ (class I or IIa), it is important to realize thatmany patients who have received appropriate risk information often
(in up to 50% of cases, some studies suggest) consciously opt to
forego the proposed intervention. This applies not only to lifestylemeasures, but also to drug interventions. Apparently, what professio-
nals feel is sufficient risk reduction for a reasonable effort or initiation
of a drug with few side-effects does not always correspond topatients’ views. The reverse is also true: not only may some patients
at (very) high risk forego interventions, some patients with low-to-
moderate risk may be highly motivated to decrease their risk evenfurther. Hence, treatment recommendations are never ‘imperative’
for (very) high risk patients, nor are interventions ever ‘prohibited’
for patients at low-to-moderate risk. There is evidence that a higherproportion of women, compared to men, have a low awareness of
their CVD risk and the need for therapeutic interventions. This war-
rants efforts to improve awareness, risk assessment, and treatment inwomen.
52,346/C0351
4.2. Optimizing cardiovascular risk
management
4.2.1. Goals of clinicianpatient communication
Clinicians should provide a personalized presentation of guidelines toimprove understanding, encourage lifestyle changes, and support
adherence to drug therapy. Applying this in daily practice faces differ-
ent barriers.
352Patients’ ability to adopt a healthy lifestyle depends
on cognitive and emotional factors, the impact of a diagnosis or symp-
toms, socioeconomic factors, educational level, and mental health.
Perceived susceptibility to illness and the anticipated severity of theconsequences are also prominent components of patients’
motivation.
353
4.2.2. How to improve motivation?
Communication strategies such as mo tivational interviewing are use-
ful.354Consultation sessions may include a family member or friend,
especially for elderly patients. Connection is paramount: focus before
greeting; listen intently; agree on what matters most; connect with theperson’s story; and explore emotions.
355The OARS (Open-ended
questions, Affirmation, Reflective li stening, and Summarizing) principle
helps patients to present their perceptions, and clinicians to summa-rize. The SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Timely)
principle may help with setting goals for behavioural change.
353,356
Healthcare professionals must consi der capability, opportunity (physi-
cal, social, or environmental) and motivation for behavioural
change.357Multidisciplinary behavioural approaches that combine the
knowledge and skills of different caregivers are recommended.358
4.2.3. Optimizing drug adherenceMedication adherence ranges from 50% for primary ASCVD preven-
tion to 66% for secondary prevention.
359Physicians should consider
non-adherence in every patient and inquire non-judgmentally aboutit.
360Approximately 9% of cases of ASCVD in Europe can be attrib-
uted to poor medication adherence.361Contributors to non-
adherence include polypharmacy, complexity of drug/dose regimes,poor doctor-patient relationship, lack of disease acceptance, beliefsabout consequences and side-effects, intellectual/cognitive abilities,
mental disorders, physical limitations, financial aspects, and living
alone.
360,362/C0364Importantly, only substantial risk reduction moti-
vates patients for preventive drug treatment, which obviates the
need for appropriate risk communication.365,366Depression is
another important factor, and adequate treatment thereof improvesadherence.
367,368
Mobile phone applications may improve adherence to both medi-
cation and behavioural changes.369Their use is easy and probably
cost-effective.370

are discussed. Table 6summarizes the treatment goals and some key
interventions for different categories of patients. For additional infor-mation on risk categories and the principle of a stepwise approach to
treatment targets, please refer to section 3.2.3.1 . For details on treat-
ment goals, how to achieve them, strengths of recommendations andlevels of supporting evidence, please go to the relevant subsections.
4.3.Optimizing lifestyle
4.3.1. Physical activity and exercise
PA reduces the risk of many adverse health outcomes and risk factors
in all ages and both sexes. There is an inverse relationship between
moderate-to-vigorous PA and all-cause mortality, CV morbidity andRecommendations for physical activity
Recommendations ClassaLevelb
It is recommended for adults of all ages to strive
for at least 150 - 300 min a week of moderate-
intensity or 75 - 150 min a week of vigorous-intensity aerobic PA, or an equivalent combina-
tion thereof, to reduce all-cause mortality, CV
mortality, and morbidity.
371,372IA
It is recommended that adults who cannot per-
form 150 min of moderate-intensity PA a week
should stay as active as their abilities and healthcondition allow.
373,374IB
It is recommended to reduce sedentary time to
engage in at least light activity throughout the
day to reduce all-cause and CV mortality andmorbidity.
375/C0377IB
Performing resistance exercise, in addition to
aerobic activity, is recommended on 2 or moredays per week to reduce all-cause
mortality.
378,379IB
Lifestyle interventions, such as group or individ-
ual education, behaviour-change techniques, tel-ephone counselling, and use of consumer-based
wearable activity trackers, should be considered
to increase PA participation.
380/C0382IIa B
CV = cardiovascular; PA = physical activity.

bLevel of evidence.

nodes.title: Risk reclassification
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the importance of individual treatment and interventions for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk management. It highlights that many patients may choose to forego recommended interventions, even when they are deemed strong recommendations by professionals. The document emphasizes the need for personalized communication between clinicians and patients to improve understanding and adherence to treatment plans. It outlines strategies to enhance patient motivation, such as motivational interviewing and involving family members in consultations. The document also addresses medication adherence, noting that non-adherence is a significant issue and can be influenced by various factors, including mental health and socioeconomic status. 

Additionally, it provides recommendations for physical activity, emphasizing the benefits of both aerobic and resistance exercises in reducing health risks. It suggests specific guidelines for physical activity levels and the importance of reducing sedentary behavior. The document concludes with a brief mention of nutrition and alcohol recommendations as essential components of CVD prevention. Overall, it underscores the need for a comprehensive, individualized approach to managing cardiovascular risk through lifestyle changes and medication adherence.

4.3.1.1 Physical activity prescriptionPA should be individually assessed and prescribed in terms of fre-quency, intensity, time (duration), type, and progression.
389
Recommendations regarding pre-participation screening can befound in previous ESC Guidelines.
388Interventions shown to increase
PA level or reduce sedentary behaviour include behaviour theory-
based interventions, such as goal-setting, re-evaluation of goals, self-
monitoring, and feedback.372,380,381Using a wearable activity tracker
may help increase PA.382Most important is to encourage activity that
people enjoy and/or can include in their daily routines, as such activ-
ities are more likely to be sustainable.
4.3.1.2 Aerobic physical activity
Examples of aerobic PA include walking, jogging, cycling, etc.389
Adults are recommended to perform at least 150 /C0300 min a week
of moderate-intensity PA, or 75 /C0150 min of vigorous-intensity PA,
or an equivalent combination of both, spread throughout theweek.
371,372Additional benefits are gained with even more PA.
Practising PA should still be encouraged in individuals unable to meet
the minimum. In sedentary individuals, a gradual increase in activitylevel is recommended. When older adults or individuals with chronic
conditions cannot achieve 150 min of moderate-intensity PA a week,
they should be as active as their abilities and conditionsallow.
371/C0375,384,385PA accumulated in bouts of even <10 min is
associated with favourable outcomes, including mortality.371,390
PA can be expressed in absolute or relative terms.389Absolute
intensity is the amount of energy expended per minute of activity,
assessed by oxygen uptake per unit of time (mL/min or L/min) or by
metabolic equivalent of task (MET). A compendium of the energycost in MET values for various activities is available.
391An absolute
measure does not consider individual factors such as body weight,
sex, and fitness level.389Relative intensity is determined based on an individual’s maximum
(peak) effort, e.g. percentage of cardiorespiratory fitness (%VO 2
max), percentage of maximum (peak) heart rate (%HR max)o ru s i n g
rating of perceived exertion according to the Borg scale. Less fit indi-
viduals generally require a higher level of effort than fitter people toperform the same activity. A relative intensity measure is necessary
to provide an individualized PA prescription.

are presented in Table 7.

risks of total CV events and all-cause mortality.378,379,393/C0395The sug-

inactive adults, light-intensity PA, even as little as 15 minutes a day, is

health outcomes.

nodes.title: Assess risk factors and cardiovascular disease risk in persons with obesity
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the importance of physical activity (PA) in reducing the risk of mortality and type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM). It emphasizes the need for individualized PA prescriptions based on frequency, intensity, time, type, and progression. The document outlines various forms of PA, including aerobic activities (e.g., walking, jogging, cycling) and resistance exercises, highlighting recommended durations and intensities for different populations, including older adults and those with chronic conditions. It also addresses the negative impact of sedentary behavior on health and suggests that even light-intensity PA can be beneficial. Additionally, the document includes a classification of physical activity intensity and provides recommendations for nutrition and alcohol consumption as part of cardiovascular disease prevention.

nodes.title: Heart failure
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers guidelines and recommendations related to physical activity (PA) and nutrition for cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention. Key points include:

1. **Physical Activity Prescription**: PA should be tailored to individuals based on frequency, intensity, time, type, and progression. Behavior-based interventions and the use of wearable activity trackers are encouraged to increase PA levels.

2. **Aerobic Physical Activity**: Adults are advised to engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity weekly, with additional benefits from higher levels of activity. Even short bouts of activity can yield positive health outcomes.

3. **Resistance Exercise**: Incorporating resistance training is linked to lower risks of cardiovascular events and mortality. Recommendations include performing 1-3 sets of exercises targeting major muscle groups at least twice a week.

4. **Sedentary Behavior**: Reducing sedentary time is crucial, as it is associated with increased risks of chronic diseases. Light-intensity PA can be beneficial for inactive adults.

5. **Nutrition and Alcohol**: A healthy diet is emphasized as essential for CVD prevention, with recommendations for a plant-based diet, reducing saturated fats, and limiting salt intake. Specific dietary components such as fatty acids, minerals, vitamins, and fiber are discussed in relation to their impact on cardiovascular health.

6. **Specific Dietary Recommendations**: The document suggests adopting a Mediterranean diet, increasing fiber intake, consuming fruits and vegetables, and limiting processed meats and sugar-sweetened beverages. Alcohol consumption should be restricted to a maximum of 100 grams per week.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of individualized PA and dietary strategies in reducing cardiovascular risk and promoting overall health.

Dietary habits influence CV risk, mainly through risk factors such as
lipids, BP, body weight, and DM.401,402Table 8 summarizes the char-
acteristics of a healthy diet. Although recommendations aboutnutrients and foods remain important for CV health, there is a grow-
ing concern about environmental sustainability, supporting a shift
from an animal- to a more plant-based food pattern.
411,412
4.3.2.1 Fatty acids
Risk of CHD is reduced when dietary saturated fats are replaced
appropriately ( Figure 10). This is also the case when replacing meat
and dairy foods.406,407Polyunsaturated fats (-25%), monounsaturated
fats (-15%), and to a lesser extent carbohydrates from whole grains
(-9%), were all associated with reduced CHD risk when isocaloricallysubstituted for dietary saturated fat.
408,409
Reducing saturated fatty acid intake to less than 10% of energy
may have additional benefits.405However, the LDL-C-lowering effect
of substituting polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) for saturated fatty
acids may be less in obese (5.3%) than in normal-weight persons
(9.7%).421
Trans fatty acids, formed during industrial processing of fats, have
unfavourable effects on total cholesterol (increase) and HDL-C
(decrease). On average, a 2% increase in energy intake from transfatty acids is associated with a 23% higher CHD risk.
422Ar e g u l a t i o n
of the European Union (EU) Commission has set the upper limit to 2
g per 100 g of fat (April 2019) (https://ec.europa.eu/food/safety/label-ling_nutrition/trans-fat-food_en).
When guidelines to lower saturated fat intake are followed, reduc-
tions in dietary cholesterol intake follow.
4.3.2.2 Minerals and vitamins
A reduction in sodium intake may reduce SBP by, on average, 5.8mmHg in hypertensive, and 1.9 mmHg in normotensive patients.
410The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) trial showed
a dose /C0response relation between sodium reduction and BP
reduction.423In a meta-analysis, salt reduction of 2.5 g/day resulted in
a 20% reduction of ASCVD events (RR 0.80).410AU -o rJ - s h a p e d
relation between a low salt intake and ASCVD is debated.424
Underlying illness and malnutrition may explain both low food and
salt intakes as well as increased ASCVD.410,425,426The totality of evi-
dence warrants salt reduction to prevent CHD and stroke.
In most Western countries, salt intake is high ( /C259/C010 g/day),
whereas the recommended maximum intake is 5 g/day. Optimal
intake might be as low as /C253 g/day. Salt reduction can be achieved by
dietary choices (fewer processed foods) and the reformulation offoods by lowering their salt content (see section 5.2.2 ).
Potassium (e.g. in fruits and vegetables) has favourable effects on
BP and risk of stroke (RR 0.76).
427
As for vitamins, observational studies have found inverse associa-
tions between vitamins A and E and risk of ASCVD. However, inter-
vention trials have failed to confirm these findings. Also, trials ofsupplementation with B vitamins (B6, folic acid, and B12), and vita-
mins C and D have not shown beneficial effects.
428,429
4.3.2.3 Fibre
Each 7 g/day higher intake of total fibre is associated with a 9% lower
risk of CAD (RR 0.91).430A 10 g/day higher fibre intake was associ-
ated with a 16% lower risk of stroke (RR 0.84) and a 6% lower risk of
type 2 DM (RR 0.94).431,432A high fibre intake may reduce postpran-
dial glucose responses after carbohydrate-rich meals and also lowertriglyceride levels.
433

nodes.title: Cancer
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the impact of dietary habits on cardiovascular (CV) risk, emphasizing the role of various nutrients and food patterns. Key points include:

1. **Dietary Influence on CV Risk**: Dietary habits affect cardiovascular risk factors such as lipids, blood pressure (BP), body weight, and diabetes mellitus (DM). A shift towards a more plant-based diet is recommended for both health and environmental sustainability.

2. **Fatty Acids**: Replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats can reduce the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). Trans fatty acids are linked to increased CHD risk, and guidelines recommend limiting their intake.

3. **Minerals and Vitamins**: Reducing sodium intake can lower blood pressure, with evidence supporting salt reduction to prevent cardiovascular disease (CVD). Potassium intake from fruits and vegetables is beneficial, while the effects of vitamin supplementation on CVD risk remain inconclusive.

4. **Fibre**: Higher fibre intake is associated with lower risks of coronary artery disease (CAD), stroke, and type 2 diabetes. 

5. **Specific Foods and Food Groups**: The document highlights the benefits of consuming fruits, vegetables, pulses, nuts, and fish, while recommending reduced intake of red and processed meats. It also discusses the limited benefits of fish oil supplements and the risks associated with alcohol consumption.

6. **Recommendations**: The document provides dietary recommendations, including adopting a Mediterranean diet, limiting saturated fat and salt intake, increasing plant-based foods, and moderating alcohol consumption.

Overall, the document underscores the importance of dietary choices in managing cardiovascular health and reducing disease risk.

nodes.title: Diagnosis and screening
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses dietary recommendations and their associations with cardiovascular health. It highlights the benefits of consuming fruits and vegetables, with an emphasis on achieving at least five servings per day to lower the risk of stroke and all-cause mortality. The document also addresses the positive impact of daily nut and pulse consumption on cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in lowering LDL cholesterol levels. It recommends reducing meat intake, especially processed meat, while suggesting that substituting red meat with plant-based foods can improve health outcomes. The role of fish consumption is examined, noting that eating fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids may reduce the risk of coronary artery disease and stroke, although fish oil supplements show mixed results in clinical studies. Lastly, the document discusses alcohol consumption, indicating that exceeding 100 grams of pure alcohol per week can negatively affect life expectancy and cardiovascular health, challenging the notion that moderate alcohol intake is protective against heart disease.

nodes.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses dietary recommendations and their impact on cardiovascular health. Key points include:

1. **Fruits and Vegetables**: Daily intake of three to five servings is associated with lower risks of stroke and coronary heart disease (CHD), with no additional benefits beyond five servings.

2. **Pulses and Nuts**: Regular consumption of pulses can lower LDL cholesterol and reduce coronary heart disease risk. Daily intake of mixed nuts is linked to a significant reduction in the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

3. **Meat Consumption**: Lowering meat intake, particularly processed meat, is advised for health and environmental reasons. Substituting red meat with plant-based foods can improve cholesterol levels.

4. **Fish**: Eating fish, especially those high in omega-3 fatty acids, is associated with reduced risks of coronary artery disease (CAD) and stroke, although fish oil supplements show mixed results in clinical outcomes.

5. **Alcohol**: Moderate alcohol consumption has a complex relationship with cardiovascular disease, with evidence suggesting that abstainers may have lower risks compared to moderate drinkers.

6. **Sugary Beverages**: High consumption of sugar-sweetened drinks is linked to increased CAD risk, while artificially sweetened beverages show different associations.

7. **Coffee**: Non-filtered coffee may increase ASCVD mortality risk, but moderate consumption is generally considered safe.

8. **Functional Foods**: Foods containing phytosterols can lower LDL cholesterol, but clinical endpoint studies are lacking.

9. **Dietary Patterns**: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with significant reductions in cardiovascular incidence and mortality.

10. **Weight Management**: Emphasizes the importance of weight loss for reducing cardiovascular risk, with various dietary approaches discussed, including Mediterranean and low-carbohydrate diets. Long-term maintenance of a healthy diet is crucial for sustained benefits.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of dietary choices in managing cardiovascular health and the need for balanced, plant-based diets.

some espresso coffees. Moderate coffee consumption (3 /C04 cups

4.3.2.4.8. Functional foods. Functional foods containing phytosterols
(plant sterols and stanols) are effective in lowering LDL-C levels by
an average of 10% when consumed in amounts of 2 g/day.448The
effect is in addition to that obtained with a low-fat diet or use of sta-
tins. No studies with clinical endpoints have been performed yet.
Red yeast rice supplements are not recommended and may even
cause side-effects.449
4.3.2.4.9. Dietary patterns. Studying the impact of a total dietary pat-tern shows the full preventive potential of diet. The Mediterraneandiet includes high intakes of fruits, vegetables, pulses, wholegrain
products, fish, and olive oil, moderate consumption of alcohol, and
low consumption of (red) meat, dairy products, and saturated fattyacids. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a
10% reduction in CV incidence or mortality and an 8% reduction in
all-cause mortality.
403Following a Mediterranean diet enriched with
nuts over a 5-year period, compared with a control diet, lowered the
risk of ASCVD by 28% and by 31% with a diet enriched with extra-
virgin olive oil.404
Also, a shift from a more animal-based to a plant-based food pat-
tern may reduce ASCVD.411
4.3.3. Body weight and composition4.3.3.1 Treatment goals and modalities
Although diet, exercise, and behaviour modification are the main
therapies for overweight and obesity, they are often unsuccessful inthe long term. Yet, maintaining even a moderate weight loss of
5 - 10% from baseline has salutary effects on risk factors including BP,
lipids, and glycaemic control,
450,451as well as on premature all-cause
mortality.456Weight loss is associated with lower morbidity but
higher mortality in (biologically) older adults (the ‘obesity paradox’).
In this group, emphasis should be less on weight loss and more onmaintaining muscle mass and good nutrition.
4.3.3.2 Diets for weight loss
Energy restriction is the cornerstone of management. PA is essential
to maintain weight loss and prevent rebound weight gain, but is not
reviewed here. Hypocaloric diets may be categorized as:
1. Diets that aim to reduce ASCVD, including plant-based457,458and
hypocaloric Mediterranean diets,458,459with modifications to suit
local food availability and preferences.
2. Changes to the fat and carbohydrate macronutrient composition of
the diet, including low or very low carbohydrate diets (with
50/C0130 g and 20 /C049 g carbohydrates/day, respectively), moderate
carbohydrate diets (>130 /C0225 g carbohydrates/day), and low-fat
diets (<30% of energy from fat).
3. High-protein diets to preserve lean muscle mass and enhance
satiety.
4. Diets focusing on specific food groups (e.g. increasing fruit and vege-
tables or avoiding refined sugars).
5. Diets that restrict energy intake for specified time periods, for
example on 2 days a week or alternate days (intermittent fasting) or
during certain hours of the day (time-restricted eating).
These diets give broadly similar short-term weight loss.452/C0454By
12 months, the effects tend to diminish.453Benefits of the
Mediterranean diet, however, tend to persist. The quality of nutrients
in a diet, for example substituting unsaturated for saturated fats (see
section 4.3.2.1 ) and including fibre-rich carbohydrates460determines
whether a diet is healthy in the long term.
Low or very low carbohydrate diets may have advantages regard-
ing appetite control, lowering triglycerides, and reducing medicationsfor type 2 DM.
461Such diets may be ketogenic and need medical or
at least dietetic supervision. Studies beyond 2 years are scarce.
Extreme carbohydrate intakes should be avoided in the long termand plant substitutions of fat and protein for carbohydrates are
advantageous over animal ones.
462
Intermittent fasting diets produce equivalent weight loss to contin-
uous energy restriction when matched for energy intake.463

nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various dietary factors and their associations with cardiovascular disease (CVD) and overall health. Key points include:

1. **Soft Drinks and Sugar**: Regular consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is linked to a higher risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) in women, while artificially sweetened beverages show no such association. The World Health Organization recommends limiting free sugar intake to 10% of total energy.

2. **Coffee**: Non-filtered coffee may increase the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) mortality, while moderate consumption is likely not harmful and may even be beneficial.

3. **Functional Foods**: Foods containing phytosterols can lower LDL cholesterol levels, but red yeast rice supplements are not recommended due to potential side effects.

4. **Dietary Patterns**: The Mediterranean diet, rich in fruits, vegetables, and healthy fats, is associated with reduced cardiovascular incidence and mortality. Shifting from animal-based to plant-based diets may also lower ASCVD risk.

5. **Body Weight and Composition**: Weight management strategies focus on diet, exercise, and behavior modification, with even modest weight loss providing health benefits. Various diets for weight loss are discussed, including plant-based, low-carbohydrate, and intermittent fasting diets, with an emphasis on maintaining a healthy diet over time.

6. **Recommendations**: Overweight and obese individuals are advised to aim for weight reduction to improve cardiovascular risk factors, and bariatric surgery may be considered for those who do not achieve sustained weight loss through lifestyle changes.

.......................................................................................................................................................4.3.2.4.6. Soft drinks and sugar. Regular consumption of sugar-
sweetened beverages (i.e. two servings per day compared with one
serving per month) was associated with a 35% higher risk of CAD in
women in the Nurses’ Health Study, whereas artificially sweetenedbeverages were not associated with CAD. In the EPIC (European
Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition) cohort, both arti-
ficially and sugar-sweetened soft dr inks were associated with all-cause
mortality, while only the former wa s associated with circulatory dis-
eases.
419The WHO guideline recommends a maximum intake of 10%
of energy from free sugars (mono- and disaccharides), which includes
added sugars as well as sugars present in fruit juices.420
4.3.2.4.7. Coffee. Non-filtered coffee contains LDL-C-raising cafestol
and kahweol, and may be associated with an up to 25% increased risk
of ASCVD mortality by consumption of nine or more drinks a day.446
Non-filtered coffee includes boiled, Greek, and Turkish coffee and
some espresso coffees. Moderate coffee consumption (3 /C04 cups
per day) is probably not harmful, perhaps even moderatelybeneficial.
447
4.3.2.4.8. Functional foods. Functional foods containing phytosterols
(plant sterols and stanols) are effective in lowering LDL-C levels by
an average of 10% when consumed in amounts of 2 g/day.448The
effect is in addition to that obtained with a low-fat diet or use of sta-
tins. No studies with clinical endpoints have been performed yet.
Red yeast rice supplements are not recommended and may even
cause side-effects.449
4.3.2.4.9. Dietary patterns. Studying the impact of a total dietary pat-tern shows the full preventive potential of diet. The Mediterraneandiet includes high intakes of fruits, vegetables, pulses, wholegrain
products, fish, and olive oil, moderate consumption of alcohol, and
low consumption of (red) meat, dairy products, and saturated fattyacids. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a
10% reduction in CV incidence or mortality and an 8% reduction in
all-cause mortality.
403Following a Mediterranean diet enriched with
nuts over a 5-year period, compared with a control diet, lowered the
risk of ASCVD by 28% and by 31% with a diet enriched with extra-
virgin olive oil.404
Also, a shift from a more animal-based to a plant-based food pat-
tern may reduce ASCVD.411
4.3.3. Body weight and composition4.3.3.1 Treatment goals and modalities
Although diet, exercise, and behaviour modification are the main
therapies for overweight and obesity, they are often unsuccessful inthe long term. Yet, maintaining even a moderate weight loss of
5 - 10% from baseline has salutary effects on risk factors including BP,
lipids, and glycaemic control,
450,451as well as on premature all-cause
mortality.456Weight loss is associated with lower morbidity but
higher mortality in (biologically) older adults (the ‘obesity paradox’).
In this group, emphasis should be less on weight loss and more onmaintaining muscle mass and good nutrition.
4.3.3.2 Diets for weight loss
Energy restriction is the cornerstone of management. PA is essential
to maintain weight loss and prevent rebound weight gain, but is not
reviewed here. Hypocaloric diets may be categorized as:
1. Diets that aim to reduce ASCVD, including plant-based457,458and
hypocaloric Mediterranean diets,458,459with modifications to suit
local food availability and preferences.
2. Changes to the fat and carbohydrate macronutrient composition of
the diet, including low or very low carbohydrate diets (with
50/C0130 g and 20 /C049 g carbohydrates/day, respectively), moderate
carbohydrate diets (>130 /C0225 g carbohydrates/day), and low-fat
diets (<30% of energy from fat).
3. High-protein diets to preserve lean muscle mass and enhance
satiety.
4. Diets focusing on specific food groups (e.g. increasing fruit and vege-
tables or avoiding refined sugars).
5. Diets that restrict energy intake for specified time periods, for
example on 2 days a week or alternate days (intermittent fasting) or
during certain hours of the day (time-restricted eating).
These diets give broadly similar short-term weight loss.452/C0454By
12 months, the effects tend to diminish.453Benefits of the
Mediterranean diet, however, tend to persist. The quality of nutrients
in a diet, for example substituting unsaturated for saturated fats (see
section 4.3.2.1 ) and including fibre-rich carbohydrates460determines
whether a diet is healthy in the long term.
Low or very low carbohydrate diets may have advantages regard-
ing appetite control, lowering triglycerides, and reducing medicationsfor type 2 DM.
461Such diets may be ketogenic and need medical or
at least dietetic supervision. Studies beyond 2 years are scarce.
Extreme carbohydrate intakes should be avoided in the long termand plant substitutions of fat and protein for carbohydrates are
advantageous over animal ones.
462
Intermittent fasting diets produce equivalent weight loss to contin-
uous energy restriction when matched for energy intake.463
Medications approved in Europe as aids to weight loss (orlistat,
naltrexone/bupropion, high-dose liraglutide) may supplementlifestyle change to achieve weight loss and maintenance, althoughRecommendations for body weight
Recommendations ClassaLevelb
It is recommended that overweight and obese
people aim for a reduction in weight to reduce
BP, dyslipidaemia, and risk of type 2 DM, andthus improve their CVD risk proﬁle.
450,451IA
While a range of diets are effective for weight
loss, it is recommended that a healthy diet inregard to CVD risk is maintained over
time.
452/C0454IA
ContinuedBariatric surgery for obese high-risk individuals
should be considered when lifestyle change doesnot result in maintained weight loss.
455IIa B
CVD = cardiovascular disease; BP = blood pressure; DM = diabetes mellitus.
aClass of recommendation.
bLevel of evidence.

nodes.title: Mental disorders
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various dietary factors and lifestyle interventions related to cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Key points include:

1. **Soft Drinks and Sugar**: Regular consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is linked to a higher risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) in women, while artificially sweetened beverages show no such association. The World Health Organization recommends limiting free sugar intake to 10% of total energy.

2. **Coffee Consumption**: Non-filtered coffee may increase the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) mortality, while moderate consumption is likely safe or beneficial.

3. **Functional Foods**: Foods containing phytosterols can lower LDL cholesterol levels, but red yeast rice supplements are discouraged due to potential side effects.

4. **Dietary Patterns**: The Mediterranean diet, rich in fruits, vegetables, and healthy fats, is associated with reduced cardiovascular incidence and mortality. Shifting towards a plant-based diet may also lower ASCVD risk.

5. **Body Weight and Composition**: Weight management through diet and exercise is crucial for reducing CVD risk. Various dietary approaches, including hypocaloric and Mediterranean diets, are effective for weight loss, though long-term adherence is challenging.

6. **Mental Healthcare and Psychosocial Interventions**: Addressing unhealthy lifestyles can improve both CVD risk and mental health. Smoking cessation is highlighted as a highly effective preventive measure.

7. **Smoking Intervention**: Comprehensive strategies for smoking cessation are recommended, emphasizing that quitting smoking significantly reduces CVD risk, regardless of potential weight gain.

Overall, the document emphasizes the importance of dietary choices, weight management, and mental health in reducing cardiovascular disease risk.

serving per month) was associated with a 35% higher risk of CAD in
women in the Nurses’ Health Study, whereas artificially sweetenedbeverages were not associated with CAD. In the EPIC (European
Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition) cohort, both arti-
ficially and sugar-sweetened soft dr inks were associated with all-cause
mortality, while only the former wa s associated with circulatory dis-
eases.
419The WHO guideline recommends a maximum intake of 10%
of energy from free sugars (mono- and disaccharides), which includes
added sugars as well as sugars present in fruit juices.420
4.3.2.4.7. Coffee. Non-filtered coffee contains LDL-C-raising cafestol
and kahweol, and may be associated with an up to 25% increased risk
of ASCVD mortality by consumption of nine or more drinks a day.446
Non-filtered coffee includes boiled, Greek, and Turkish coffee and
some espresso coffees. Moderate coffee consumption (3 /C04 cups
per day) is probably not harmful, perhaps even moderatelybeneficial.
447
4.3.2.4.8. Functional foods. Functional foods containing phytosterols
(plant sterols and stanols) are effective in lowering LDL-C levels by
an average of 10% when consumed in amounts of 2 g/day.448The
effect is in addition to that obtained with a low-fat diet or use of sta-
tins. No studies with clinical endpoints have been performed yet.
Red yeast rice supplements are not recommended and may even
cause side-effects.449
4.3.2.4.9. Dietary patterns. Studying the impact of a total dietary pat-tern shows the full preventive potential of diet. The Mediterraneandiet includes high intakes of fruits, vegetables, pulses, wholegrain
products, fish, and olive oil, moderate consumption of alcohol, and
low consumption of (red) meat, dairy products, and saturated fattyacids. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a
10% reduction in CV incidence or mortality and an 8% reduction in
all-cause mortality.
403Following a Mediterranean diet enriched with
nuts over a 5-year period, compared with a control diet, lowered the
risk of ASCVD by 28% and by 31% with a diet enriched with extra-
virgin olive oil.404
Also, a shift from a more animal-based to a plant-based food pat-
tern may reduce ASCVD.411
4.3.3. Body weight and composition4.3.3.1 Treatment goals and modalities
Although diet, exercise, and behaviour modification are the main
therapies for overweight and obesity, they are often unsuccessful inthe long term. Yet, maintaining even a moderate weight loss of
5 - 10% from baseline has salutary effects on risk factors including BP,
lipids, and glycaemic control,
450,451as well as on premature all-cause
mortality.456Weight loss is associated with lower morbidity but
higher mortality in (biologically) older adults (the ‘obesity paradox’).
In this group, emphasis should be less on weight loss and more onmaintaining muscle mass and good nutrition.
4.3.3.2 Diets for weight loss
Energy restriction is the cornerstone of management. PA is essential
to maintain weight loss and prevent rebound weight gain, but is not
reviewed here. Hypocaloric diets may be categorized as:
1. Diets that aim to reduce ASCVD, including plant-based457,458and
hypocaloric Mediterranean diets,458,459with modifications to suit
local food availability and preferences.
2. Changes to the fat and carbohydrate macronutrient composition of
the diet, including low or very low carbohydrate diets (with
50/C0130 g and 20 /C049 g carbohydrates/day, respectively), moderate
carbohydrate diets (>130 /C0225 g carbohydrates/day), and low-fat
diets (<30% of energy from fat).
3. High-protein diets to preserve lean muscle mass and enhance
satiety.
4. Diets focusing on specific food groups (e.g. increasing fruit and vege-
tables or avoiding refined sugars).
5. Diets that restrict energy intake for specified time periods, for
example on 2 days a week or alternate days (intermittent fasting) or
during certain hours of the day (time-restricted eating).
These diets give broadly similar short-term weight loss.452/C0454By
12 months, the effects tend to diminish.453Benefits of the
Mediterranean diet, however, tend to persist. The quality of nutrients
in a diet, for example substituting unsaturated for saturated fats (see
section 4.3.2.1 ) and including fibre-rich carbohydrates460determines
whether a diet is healthy in the long term.
Low or very low carbohydrate diets may have advantages regard-
ing appetite control, lowering triglycerides, and reducing medicationsfor type 2 DM.
461Such diets may be ketogenic and need medical or
at least dietetic supervision. Studies beyond 2 years are scarce.
Extreme carbohydrate intakes should be avoided in the long termand plant substitutions of fat and protein for carbohydrates are
advantageous over animal ones.
462
Intermittent fasting diets produce equivalent weight loss to contin-
uous energy restriction when matched for energy intake.463

nodes.title: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various treatment options and interventions for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and associated mental health issues. Key points include:

1. **Medication-Assisted Weight Loss**: Meta-analysis shows positive effects on blood pressure, glycaemic control, and mortality related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

2. **Bariatric Surgery**: This is highlighted as an effective treatment for extreme obesity, significantly reducing mortality risks compared to non-surgical patients.

3. **Mental Healthcare and Psychosocial Interventions**: Emphasizes the importance of addressing unhealthy lifestyles to reduce CVD risk and improve mental health. Smoking cessation, exercise, and dietary changes are beneficial. Mental disorders increase CVD risk, and effective treatments for depression can lower this risk.

4. **Psychological Interventions**: Various studies indicate that psychological therapies can improve outcomes for patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) and reduce mortality rates.

5. **Smoking Cessation**: Stopping smoking is identified as a highly effective preventive measure against CVD, with significant health benefits even for heavy smokers. Recommendations for smoking cessation strategies include support and pharmacotherapy.

6. **Recommendations for Mental Healthcare**: Specific recommendations are provided for managing patients with mental disorders and ASCVD, including the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for those with major depression.

7. **Interdisciplinary Cooperation**: The document stresses the need for collaboration among healthcare providers when treating ASCVD patients with complex mental health issues, particularly those on psychiatric medications that may increase cardiac risks. 

Overall, the document underscores the interconnectedness of mental health and cardiovascular health, advocating for comprehensive treatment approaches.

nodes.title: Obstetric conditions
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various interventions for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, particularly in patients with obesity and mental health disorders. Key points include:

1. **Medication-Assisted Weight Loss**: Meta-analysis shows positive effects on blood pressure, glycaemic control, and mortality related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

2. **Bariatric Surgery**: This is highlighted as an effective treatment for extreme obesity, significantly reducing mortality risks compared to non-surgical counterparts.

3. **Mental Healthcare and Psychosocial Interventions**: Emphasizes the importance of addressing unhealthy lifestyles to improve both CVD risk and mental health. Smoking cessation, exercise, and dietary changes are beneficial. Mental disorders increase CVD risk, and effective treatments for depression can lower this risk.

4. **Psychological Interventions**: Evidence suggests that psychological therapies can improve outcomes in coronary heart disease (CHD) patients, reducing mortality and recurrent events.

5. **Smoking Cessation**: Identified as a critical preventive measure, with significant health benefits, including reduced myocardial infarction and mortality rates. Recommendations for smoking cessation strategies are provided, emphasizing the need for support and various therapeutic options.

6. **Recommendations for Care**: The document outlines specific recommendations for managing patients with mental disorders and CVD, including the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for those with major depression, while cautioning against certain antidepressants in heart failure patients.

Overall, the document underscores the interconnectedness of mental health, lifestyle changes, and cardiovascular health, advocating for comprehensive and interdisciplinary approaches to treatment.

nodes.title: Non-obstetric conditions
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various treatment options and interventions for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and associated mental health issues. Key points include:

1. **Medication-Assisted Weight Loss**: Meta-analysis shows positive effects on blood pressure, glycaemic control, and mortality related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

2. **Bariatric Surgery**: This is highlighted as an effective treatment for extreme obesity, significantly reducing mortality risks compared to non-surgical patients.

3. **Mental Healthcare and Psychosocial Interventions**: Emphasizes the importance of addressing unhealthy lifestyles to reduce CVD risk and improve mental health. Smoking cessation, exercise, and dietary changes are beneficial. Mental disorders increase CVD risk, and effective treatments for depression can lower this risk.

4. **Psychological Interventions**: Various studies indicate that psychological therapies can improve outcomes for patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) and reduce mortality rates.

5. **Smoking Cessation**: Stopping smoking is identified as a highly effective preventive measure against CVD, with significant health benefits even for heavy smokers. Recommendations for smoking cessation strategies include support and pharmacotherapy.

6. **Recommendations for Mental Healthcare**: Patients with mental disorders should receive enhanced support for lifestyle changes and medication adherence. Specific antidepressant treatments are recommended for patients with CHD and depression, while caution is advised for those with heart failure.

7. **Interdisciplinary Cooperation**: The document stresses the need for collaboration among healthcare providers when treating ASCVD patients with complex mental health issues, particularly those on psychiatric medications that may increase cardiac risks.

nodes.title: Treatment recommendations: classes, grades, and freedom of choice
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses various interventions for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, particularly focusing on obesity, mental health, smoking cessation, and lipid management. Key points include:

1. **Medication-Assisted Weight Loss**: Meta-analysis shows positive effects on blood pressure, glycaemic control, and mortality related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

2. **Bariatric Surgery**: This is highlighted as an effective treatment for extreme obesity, significantly reducing mortality risks compared to non-surgical counterparts.

3. **Mental Healthcare and Psychosocial Interventions**: Emphasizes the importance of addressing unhealthy lifestyles to improve both cardiovascular and mental health. Smoking cessation, exercise, and dietary changes are beneficial. Mental disorders increase CVD risk, and effective treatments for depression can lower this risk.

4. **Psychotherapy and Cardiac Rehabilitation**: Psychological interventions can reduce cardiac mortality and improve outcomes in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD). Collaborative care for patients with CHD and depression shows beneficial effects.

5. **Smoking Cessation**: Stopping smoking is identified as a highly effective preventive measure against CVD. Recommendations include providing support and pharmacological aids for cessation, with evidence supporting the efficacy of nicotine replacement therapy and medications like varenicline and bupropion.

6. **Lipid Management**: Discusses the role of LDL cholesterol in atherogenesis and the importance of lowering LDL levels to reduce CVD risk. Non-fasting lipid measurements are recommended for general screening.

Overall, the document underscores the interconnectedness of lifestyle factors, mental health, and medical interventions in managing cardiovascular health.

Quitting must be encouraged in all smokers, and passive smoking
should be avoided as much as possible. Very brief advice may be
advantageous when time is limited ( Table 9). A major impetus for ces-
sation occurs at the time of diagnosis or treatment of CVD.
Prompting a person to try to quit, brief reiteration of CV and other
benefits of quitting, and agreeing on a specific plan with a follow-uparrangement are evidence-based interventions.
Smokers who quit may expect an average weight gain of 5 kg, but
the health benefits of tobacco cessation outweigh risks from weight
gain.
495Persistent or reuptake of smoking is common in patients with
CHD, in particular in those with severe depression and environmen-
tal exposures.498Mood-management therapies may improve out-
comes in patients with current or past depression.499
4.5.2. Evidence-based drug interventionsDrug support for stopping smoking should be considered in all smokers
who are ready to undertake this action. Evidence-based drug interven-
tions include nicotine-replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, vareni-cline, and cytisine (not widely available).
489/C0491All forms of NRT
(chewing gum, transdermal nicotine patches, nasal spray, inhaler, sublin-
gual tablets) are effective. Combin ation vs. single-form NRT and 4 mg
vs. 2 mg gum can increase success.492NRT shows no adverse effects in
patients with ASCVD,493but evidence of efficacy in this group is incon-
clusive.494In patients with ASCVD, varenicline (RR 2.6), bupropion (RR
1.4), telephone therapy (RR 1.5), and individual counselling (RR 1.6) all
increase success rates.494The antidepressant, bupropion, aids long-
term smoking cessation with similar efficacy to NRT.490
Varenicline 1 mg b.i.d. (twice a day) increases quitting rates more
than two-fold compared with placebo.491The RR for abstinence vs.
NRT was 1.25 and vs. bupropion, 1.4. Lower or variable doses arealso effective and reduce side-effects. Varenicline beyond the 12-
week standard regimen is well tolerated. Varenicline initiated in hos-
pital following ACS is efficacious and safe.
500
The main side-effect of varenicline is nausea, but this usually sub-
sides. A causal link between varenicline and neuropsychiatric adverse
events is unlikely.501Varenicline, bupropion, and NRT do not
increase serious CV adverse event risks during or after treatment.502
Cytisine is effective for smoking cessation, but evidence to date is
limited.491
4.5.2.1 Electronic cigarettesElectronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) simulate combustible cigarettesby heating nicotine and other chemicals into a vapour. E-cigarettesdeliver nicotine without most of the tobacco chemicals, and are
probably less harmful than tobacco.
Recent evidence suggests that e-cigarettes are probably more
effective than NRT in terms of smoking cessation.
503/C0505The long-
term effects of e-cigarettes on CV and pulmonary health, however,
require more research.506Dual use with cigarettes should be
avoided. Furthermore, as e-cigarettes are addictive, their use should
be subject to similar marketing controls as standard cigarettes, espe-
cially the flavoured varieties that appeal to children.507Despite being
lower in toxicants than regular cigarettes, ‘heat-not-burn’ cigarettes
do contain tobacco and should be discouraged.
4.6. Lipids
This section covers recommendations for the diagnosis and treat-ment of unfavourable blood lipid levels. More detail and guidance for
complex cases/tertiary care, including genetic lipid disorders, areavailable in the 2019 ESC/European Atherosclerosis Society (EAS)
Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias.
3
Recent evidence has confirmed that the key initiating event in athe-
rogenesis is the retention of LDL and other cholesterol-rich lipopro-
teins within the arterial wall. The causal role of LDL-C, and other apo-
B-containing lipoproteins, in the development of ASCVD is demon-strated beyond any doubt by genetic, observational, and interven-
tional studies.
20Meta-analysis of clinical trials has indicated that the
relative reduction in CVD risk is proportional to the absolute reduc-tion of LDL-C, irrespective of the drug(s) used to achieve such
change, with no evidence of a lower limit for LDL-C values or ‘J-curve’
effect.
21The absolute benefit of lowering LDL-C depends on the
absolute risk of ASCVD and the absolute reduction in LDL-C, so
even a small absolute reduction in LDL-C may translate to significant
absolute risk reduction in a high- or very-high-risk patient.22A recent
LDL-C target-driven RCT in patients after ischaemic stroke or transi-
ent ischaemic attack (TIA) demonstrated a target LDL-C level of <1.8
mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with the use of statin and, if required, ezetimibe,was associated with a lower CVD risk than those who had a target
range of 2.3 /C02.8 mmol/L (90 /C0110 mg/dL).
508Studies on the clinical
safety of (very) low achieved LDL-C values have not caused particularconcerns, although monitoring for longer periods is required.
4.6.1. Measurement of lipids and lipoproteins
4.6.1.1 Fasting vs. non-fasting measurements
Non-fasting sampling of lipid parameters is recommended for general
risk screening, since it has the same prognostic value as fasting sam-ples.
509,510In patients with metabolic syndrome, DM, or hypertrigly-
ceridaemia, calculated LDL-C from non-fasting samples should be
interpreted with care.

It highlights the effectiveness of brief advice during clinical encounters, particularly at the time of cardiovascular disease (CVD) diagnosis or treatment. Evidence-based interventions such as nicotine-replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, and varenicline are recommended for smokers ready to quit, with specific details on their efficacy and safety. The document also addresses the role of electronic cigarettes, noting their potential as a less harmful alternative to traditional smoking, while cautioning against dual use and the need for regulatory controls. Additionally, it covers recommendations for managing blood lipid levels, emphasizing the causal relationship between low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and the importance of achieving target LDL-C levels to reduce CVD risk. The document concludes with guidance on lipid measurement, advocating for non-fasting assessments for general risk screening.
